title: Split Decision
tagline: Pick the splitter that lights every home: not too dark, not too bright.

sources.title: ITU-T G.9807.1 (02/2023), 10-Gigabit-capable symmetric passive optical network (XGS-PON)
sources.section: Annex B, clause B.6.1, Table B.6.1
sources.claim: Loss classes: N1 has a minimum of 14 dB and a maximum of 29 dB; N2 a minimum of 16 dB and a maximum of 31 dB. Where an architecture gives less than the class minimum, the network must add optical attenuators to protect receivers.

sources.title: ITU-T G.9807.1 (02/2023), 10-Gigabit-capable symmetric passive optical network (XGS-PON)
sources.section: Annex B, clauses B.9.2.6.1 and B.9.2.8.1; Tables B.9.2, B.9.3 and B.9.4
sources.claim: The attenuation range applies between the OLT and ONU reference points and includes splices, connectors, optical attenuators and other passive devices. Paths on one PON may differ by at most 15 dB. Downstream is 1575 to 1580 nm and upstream 1260 to 1280 nm.

sources.title: ITU-T G.652 (08/2024), Characteristics of a single-mode optical fibre and cable
sources.section: Appendix I, Table I.1; clause 8, Table 2, Note 2
sources.claim: Typical link attenuation is 0.5 dB/km for 1260 to 1360 nm and 0.35 dB/km for 1565 to 1625 nm. The G.652.D cable maximum is 0.40 dB/km from 1310 to 1625 nm, plus 0.07 dB/km to extend the range to 1260 nm.

sources.title: The FOA Reference Guide: Guidelines On What Loss To Expect When Testing Fiber Optic Cables
sources.claim: A typical connector loses about 0.3 dB. TIA-568 allows up to 0.75 dB for a mated pair and 0.3 dB for a splice.

sources.title: The FOA Reference Guide: Using Attenuators With Fiber Optic Data Links
sources.claim: A receiver overloads when the cable plant loses less than a minimum. An attenuator adds the missing loss.

sources.title: TEC GR/TX/OPT-001/01/APR-12, Generic Requirements for optical splitters
sources.claim: One published set of maximum splitter insertion losses: 4.0, 7.1, 10.5, 13.8, 17.1 and 20.5 dB for 1×2 to 1×64. The game's rule of 3.5 dB for each two-way split is within about half a dB of each.

rule: An ONT's optical path loss is the sum, in dB, of everything between the OLT port and that ONT: fiber, connector pairs, fusion splices, splitters and attenuators.
Every ONT must land inside the loss window of the PON's class, limits included. N1 runs from {min:N1} to {max:N1}. N2 runs from {min:N2} to {max:N2}.
Over the maximum, too little light arrives and the ONT is too dark. Under the minimum, too much light arrives and the ONT is too bright.
Among the designs that keep every ONT inside the window, the one that serves the most homes is the answer.
assumptions: The loss card holds the job's planning values, not measurements: fiber {fiber} per km, a connector pair {connector}, a fusion splice {splice}, each two-way split {splitter:2}, attenuators at the value printed on them.
The ONTs drawn are the nearest and the farthest on the PON. Every other home lies between them.
leftOut: A real design checks each direction at its own wavelength. Fiber loses more per km upstream (1260 to 1280 nm) than downstream (1575 to 1580 nm). The game uses one value, the higher one, for both.
A real budget keeps margin for repairs and ageing. The game keeps none, so every number on screen comes from an element you can see.
Transmitter power, receiver sensitivity, reflectance, bend loss and the differences between a splitter's ports are not modeled.
XGS-PON has other loss classes (B+, C+, E1, E2) and a maximum fiber distance. The game uses N1 and N2 only.
The standard also limits how far apart the losses of two paths on one PON may be. The game does not test that limit on its own; every answer in the game is within it.

levels.title: Add it up
levels.outcome: Work out one ONT's optical path loss and compare it with the class maximum.
levels.practiced: Adding every loss on a path, small ones included, and testing the total against the maximum.

intro: Welcome to Saguaro Valley. You design the outside plant of its new fiber network: the glass, the splitters and the connections between the provider's OLT and each customer's ONT.

Light leaves the OLT port and loses strength at everything it passes. Each loss is counted in decibels (dB), and decibels simply add up. The total from the OLT port to one ONT is that ONT's optical path loss.

Every PON has a loss window. For the N1 class it runs from {min:N1} to {max:N1}. In this level you need only the top of it: when a path loses more than {max:N1}, too little light arrives and the ONT is too dark.

A splitter shares one fiber among many homes, and that sharing is the largest loss on the path. More homes on one OLT port means a cheaper network, so the question is always the same: what is the largest splitter the farthest home can carry?

The loss card holds this job's planning values. The game uses one fiber value for both directions and keeps no spare margin; a real design checks each direction and keeps some. Model and sources, at the top of the page, lists everything that is left out.

terms.meaning: Optical line terminal: the provider's end of the PON. One OLT port lights one PON.
Optical network terminal: the box at the customer's end. The standard calls it an ONU.
A passive device that divides one fiber's light among several. A 1:32 splitter serves 32 homes and costs {splitter:32} on the loss card.
Two connectors mated in an adapter, as at a patch panel: {connector} for the pair.
Two fibers fused end to end: {splice} each.
Decibel. A loss in dB adds to the other losses on the same path.
The least and the most loss a PON's optics can work with. N1: {min:N1} to {max:N1}.

levels.title: The farthest home sets the limit
levels.outcome: Apply the loss window to every ONT on a PON and compare competing designs.
levels.practiced: Budgeting for the highest-loss ONT, and adding the losses of splitters in series.

intro: One splitter serves many homes, and each home has its own path: the same OLT port, the same splitter, a different drop. Every one of those paths has to land inside the window.
You do not have to work out all of them. The ONT with the most fiber, connectors and splices has the highest loss. If that ONT is at or under the maximum, so is every ONT with less loss.
These PONs use N2 optics. The N2 window runs from {min:N2} to {max:N2}, a little higher than N1 at both ends.

Splitters can also be put in series: a small one at a cabinet feeding larger ones nearer the homes. The homes multiply, so a 1:4 followed by a 1:16 serves 64. The losses add: {splitter:4} + {splitter:16}. Splitting in two stages does not save light. You pay for both.

terms.meaning: The fiber from the OLT port to the first splitter. Every home on the PON shares it.
The last piece of fiber, from a splitter to one home.
Splitters in series. Multiply the ratios to count the homes; add the losses.
A loss class with stronger optics than N1. Window: {min:N2} to {max:N2}.

levels.title: Too much light
levels.outcome: Recognize a path with less than the minimum loss and correct it with attenuation in the right place.
levels.practiced: Testing a path against the minimum as well as the maximum, and putting an attenuator where the excess light is.

intro: So far the danger was too little light. The window also has a floor. An ONT's receiver is built to pick up a faint signal from far away, and a signal that arrives too strong overloads it.

For N1 the floor is {min:N1}. A path that loses less than that is too bright. It happens on short routes with small splitters: an OLT in a cabinet beside the building it serves, or a business connected ahead of the main splitter.
The cure is an attenuator: a small fixed device that adds a known loss. The standard requires one wherever a path would fall below the class minimum.
Where it goes matters. At the OLT port it dims every ONT on the PON. At one ONT it dims only that ONT.

terms.meaning: A passive device that adds a fixed loss, printed on it, to everything that passes through it.
Loss under the class minimum: too much light reaches the receiver.
Loss over the class maximum: too little light reaches the receiver.

example.title: Worked example: an office beside the OLT, with a {att:olt} attenuator
example.result: Without the attenuator this path would lose only {fixed:X}, under the {min} minimum. The attenuator adds {chosen:X} and brings it to {total:X}, inside the window.

options.label: Build it as drawn
options.note: Short routes feel safe because nothing is lost on the way. That is the problem: less loss is not always safer.

options.label: Add a {att:olt} attenuator at the OLT port
options.note: The right idea, and not enough of it. A path has to reach the minimum, not just move toward it.

Add a {att:olt} attenuator at the OLT port
options.note: An attenuator can overshoot. Too much added loss turns a path that was too bright into one that is too dark.

hints: Add up each path as before, then compare it with both ends of the window: {min} and {max}.

rounds.goal: Choose the design that puts every ONT inside the {class} window.

options.label: Add a {att:olt} attenuator at the OLT port
options.note: An attenuator at the OLT port sits on every path. It dims the bright ONT, and it dims every other ONT by the same amount.

options.label: Add a {att:A} attenuator at ONT A
Add a {att:B} attenuator at ONT B

options.label: Build it as drawn
options.note: A PON is not finished when its farthest home works. The window applies to every ONT, the nearest included.

hints: Work out each ONT's loss as drawn, and note which side of the window each one is on. Then ask which ONTs each attenuator would affect.
As drawn, ONT A loses {fixed:A} and ONT B loses {fixed:B}. Compare each with {min} and {max}.
